analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to provide confidential advocates for sexual assault survivors and publicly report how campus assault cases are handled.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, despite 34 cosponsors including 2 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal higher-education law to combat campus sexual assault and harassment. Colleges would have to publish detailed annual statistics on rape and fondling cases, including how many were reported, how many went through campus discipline, and what sanctions resulted. Every campus would have to designate confidential sexual and interpersonal violence coordinators, adopt amnesty policies so students can report assault without being punished for their own alcohol or drug use, train staff in trauma-informed interviewing, and could face civil penalties of up to 1 percent of their operating budget for failing to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who experience domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, sexual harassment, or stalking on campus. They would gain confidential campus advocates they can talk to without triggering an official investigation, clearer information about their rights and reporting options, amnesty for related alcohol or drug violations, and national public data on how schools actually handle assault complaints.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each college to designate confidential sexual and interpersonal violence coordinators who are not required to report a complainant's identity, so survivors can get help without automatically launching an investigation.

Requires colleges to publish annual counts of reported rapes and fondling cases, how many reached the Title IX coordinator, how many went through campus discipline, how many respondents were found responsible, and what sanctions were imposed.
Requires an amnesty policy so a student who reports assault in good faith cannot be sanctioned for alcohol or drug violations revealed in the report.

Requires the Education Department to maintain a public, searchable campus safety website listing Title IX coordinators, pending investigations, and enforcement outcomes, and to offer grants (funded by penalties) to help colleges improve prevention and victim services.

Requires uniform campus-wide disciplinary processes for assault claims, ending separate tracks for student athletes or other groups, and requires written notice of any disciplinary proceeding to both the complainant and the respondent within 24 hours.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities, which would bear the cost of hiring and training coordinators, expanding reporting and record-keeping, and potential civil penalties of up to 1 percent of their operating budget for each year of noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on all institutions, including small colleges with limited staff; the bill directs the Secretary to set staffing levels by negotiated rulemaking and allows schools under 1,000 students to share coordinators, but small institutions could still face penalties of up to 1 percent of their operating budget.

The grant program has no appropriated funding: grants are awarded only 'as funds become available through the payment of penalties,' so schools with the least capacity—precisely those given grant preference—have no guaranteed money to comply.
The coordinator requirement does not take effect until at least 3 years after enactment (or earlier via rulemaking), so the core staffing protections would be delayed even if the bill had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to students—confidential advocates, amnesty, uniform discipline, and public accountability data—are substantial and targeted at a documented problem of underreporting and inconsistent campus handling of sexual assault. The main costs are administrative, falling on institutions rather than students, and the bill includes mitigations (shared coordinators for small schools, reduced penalties, voluntary resolution agreements). The biggest design weakness is that prevention grants are funded only by penalties, not appropriations. On balance, a well-constructed bill whose cost to colleges is real but modest relative to the public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on October 4, 2022, near the end of the two-year Congress, with 30 original cosponsors including Republicans John Katko and Brian Fitzpatrick.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction, and no further action—no hearing, markup, or floor vote—was ever recorded.
It finished with 34 cosponsors: 32 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber; it was never introduced in this form in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities are better off because the bill died: they avoid the new confidential-advocate staffing requirements, expanded public reporting of campus assault cases, and exposure to civil penalties of up to 1 percent of their operating budget. Students gained nothing; the status quo of campus-by-campus handling of assault complaints continued.

for.name: Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 30 original cosponsors, including two Republicans.

for.name: 31 additional cosponsors
for.role: House cosponsors (32 Democrats, 2 Republicans including John Katko and Brian Fitzpatrick)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 32 of 34 cosponsors were Democrats, joined by 2 of the chamber's Republicans; the record shows no one who actively opposed it—the bill simply never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill would impose new staffing, training, reporting, and transparency requirements, with civil penalties up to 1 percent of an institution's operating budget. Its interest in avoiding those costs ran against students' interest in confidential support and public accountability for how assault cases are handled.

industries.industry: Campus and community victim-services organizations (rape crisis centers, advocacy groups)
industries.note: The bill would let institutions partner with community-based rape crisis centers as confidential coordinators and use grant funds to strengthen victim services, creating paid roles and funding for these organizations. Their interest runs alongside survivors'.
